scenes.narration: V P C — short for virtual private cloud — networking is the domain underneath both other domains. Design Secure Architectures is the single highest-weighted section of the associate exam at thirty percent, and Design Resilient Architectures follows close behind at twenty six percent, and both of them lean on the same underlying mechanics: which subnets can reach the internet, which can't, and why a subnet spans exactly one availability zone. Get this chapter right and a surprising number of unrelated exam questions get easier too.

facts.label: Maps to two Associate domains
facts.value: Design Secure Architectures (30%) + Design Resilient Architectures (26%)

facts.label: The chapter's central claim
facts.value: Public vs. private is a route-table fact — never a subnet setting

scenes.narration: Three instincts trip people up here, and none of them are careless — they're just imported from older, on-premises networking. First, that public and private are a setting you flip, so a public I P address alone should make an instance reachable. Second, that a network address translation gateway — a NAT gateway — is a two-way bridge, since it lets traffic out, it must let traffic in. Third, that a security group needs an outbound rule mirroring every inbound rule, or response traffic could never leave. All three feel reasonable. All three are wrong, and the exam is built to catch you if you carry them in.

props.heading: "Public and private are just settings"
bullets: Believing a subnet has a public/private flag, or that a public IP address alone makes it reachable.
Assuming a NAT gateway is a two-way bridge — if it lets traffic out, surely it lets traffic in.
Assuming security groups need an outbound rule mirroring every inbound rule, like an old stateless firewall.

scenes.narration: Here's the actual rule, and it's simpler than the instinct: a subnet is public if, and only if, its route table sends all outbound traffic — the address zero dot zero dot zero dot zero, slash zero — to an Internet Gateway. Nothing else about the subnet matters. Giving an instance a public I P address in a subnet without that route changes nothing; there's simply no path for traffic to use it. And a subnet named 'private' with an accidental Internet-Gateway route is exactly as public as one that says so on the label — the route table is the only fact that counts.

cells: Public vs. private subnet
Does its route table send 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway?
Assigning the instance a public IP address
Reachable from the internet
Whether that Internet Gateway route exists at all
The subnet's name, e.g. "app-private-1a"
Outbound-only internet access
Route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway instead

scenes.narration: A NAT gateway is one-directional by design, not by accident. When a private instance opens a connection outward — say, to download a patch — the NAT gateway swaps in its own public address, forwards the request, and tracks that specific connection so the reply can find its way home. But there's no listening process on the other side waiting for the internet to knock. An unsolicited inbound request has nothing to connect to. That's the whole trap: private-subnet-plus-NAT-gateway means 'can reach out,' never 'can be reached.'

props.heading: NAT gateway: outbound yes, inbound never

rows.label: What happens
cells: NAT gateway translates the address, forwards it, and tracks the connection
There is no listener — nothing accepts a new, unsolicited session

rows.label: Result
cells: Response traffic finds its way back automatically
Request is simply dropped — by design, not misconfiguration

scenes.narration: Security groups and network ACLs — commonly just pronounced 'nackles' — are opposites on every axis that matters, and the exam almost never tests one without the other. A security group lives on the instance, remembers the state of a connection, and only ever allows — there's no deny rule type at all. A network ACL lives on the subnet, forgets everything between packets, supports an explicit deny, and evaluates its numbered rules in order until the first match wins. Forget the outbound ephemeral-port rule on a NACL and an otherwise-correct setup will silently break every response.

props.kicker: THE PAIR THE EXAM TESTS TOGETHER
props.heading: Security groups and NACLs are opposites, on purpose

rows.label: Scope
cells: Instance / ENI level
Subnet level — applies to everyone in it

rows.label: State
cells: Stateful — return traffic auto-allowed
Stateless — every direction needs its own rule

rows.label: Rule types
cells: Allow only — no deny rule exists
Allow AND deny, evaluated in numbered order

rows.label: Evaluation
cells: All matching rules apply together
First matching rule wins, rest are ignored

scenes.narration: There's a fixed order that gets almost every scenario right. Start by choosing the VPC's own address range, from a slash sixteen down to a slash twenty eight. Carve subnets out of it, one per tier per availability zone, since a subnet can never span two zones. Attach a route table to each one — at this point every subnet is private, because nothing points outward yet. Attach one Internet Gateway and route your public subnets to it. Place a NAT gateway in a public subnet and route your private subnets to that instead. And only then layer security groups and network ACLs on top, as a second, independent line of defense.

props.kicker: THE BUILD ORDER THE EXAM EXPECTS
props.heading: Six steps, each one gating the next
steps: Pick the VPC's own CIDR block, from /16 down to /28
Carve subnets — one per tier, per availability zone
Attach a route table to every subnet (all private by default)
Attach an Internet Gateway, route public subnets to it
Place a NAT gateway, route private subnets to it instead
Layer security groups and NACLs on top for defense in depth

scenes.narration: Compress the whole chapter into one table and this is it. Reach for a security group by default; reach for a network ACL specifically when you need a subnet-wide block. Reach for a NAT gateway for managed outbound access, and a Gateway V P C endpoint instead when the destination is specifically S3 or DynamoDB — no internet path required, no extra charge. VPC peering covers exactly two VPCs talking directly; the moment you need three or more to reach each other transitively, peering can't do it — that job belongs to a Transit Gateway instead.

props.heading: Choosing the right primitive for the scenario

cells: Normal two-way traffic to an instance — the default layer for almost everything
You need to explicitly block one bad actor while allowing the rest

rows.label: Network ACL
cells: A subnet-wide rule, including a genuine deny, regardless of individual security groups
You forget the numbered order or the outbound ephemeral-port rule

rows.label: NAT Gateway
cells: Reliable, managed outbound-only internet access, no server to run
Anything needs to initiate a connection in from the internet

rows.label: Gateway VPC Endpoint

The service isn't one of those exact two

Three or more VPCs need transitive reachability — peering never chains

rows.label: Transit Gateway
cells: Many VPCs (and often on-prem networks) all need to reach each other through one hub
You only have two VPCs — a single peering connection is simpler

scenes.narration: This is what a baseline VPC build actually looks like when you script it: one file for the VPC's own C I D R block, one script per subnet pinned to its availability zone, a routing folder where the public route points at the Internet Gateway and the private route points at the NAT gateway instead, and separate folders for security groups and network ACLs — because they're genuinely two different systems, not two names for the same thing.

props.heading: How a baseline VPC build is organized
lines: │   └── create-vpc.sh          # the VPC's own CIDR block
│   ├── nat-gateway.sh         # EIP + NAT gateway, in a public subnet

scenes.narration: Three commands worth being able to read cold. Describing a subnet's route tables is the fastest way to prove, from evidence rather than assumption, whether it's actually public or private — here, the private subnet's route table sends everything to a NAT gateway, not an Internet Gateway. Describing a security group shows allow-only ingress rules and, deliberately, no matching egress rule — because the group is stateful, that's not a mistake. And creating a peering connection directly between two VPCs is exactly the fix for the non-transitivity trap: you can't route through a middle VPC, so you connect the two ends directly instead.

props.heading: Confirming what you built, from the CLI

output: IpPermissionsEgress: (none defined — return traffic still allowed, stateful)
# a direct A↔C connection — not routed through B

scenes.narration: Here's a case that makes the whole chapter concrete. A logistics company's security team finds instances in a subnet literally named 'app-private-1a' reachable from the internet on port twenty two — nobody changed a security group, nobody assigned an elastic I P on purpose. The actual cause: weeks earlier, someone debugging an unrelated issue added a temporary Internet-Gateway route directly to that subnet's route table, and forgot to remove it. The subnet's name never lied on purpose — it just stopped being true the moment that one route was added. The fix isn't renaming anything; it's removing that route and auditing every other subnet's route table the same way, because a name is not evidence.

profile.name: app-private-1a
profile.role: A logistics company's subnet, named private, flagged in a routine audit
profile.detail: The audit found instances in this subnet directly reachable from the internet on port 22, even though nobody touched a security group and no instance was ever given an Elastic IP on purpose. Weeks earlier, a teammate debugging an unrelated issue had added a route sending all traffic to the Internet Gateway, directly on this subnet's route table — and never removed it.
profile.verdict: The subnet's name and its instances never changed at all. One route-table entry alone made it public — remove the errant IGW route, confirm the NAT gateway route instead, and audit every other 'private' subnet's route table the same way.

scenes.narration: Two to work through before the reveal. First: a subnet's route table has nothing but the automatic local route, and someone gives an instance in it a public I P address — does that alone make it internet-reachable? Second, a professional-level one: VPC A peers with B, and B separately peers with C — can a clever route table in B connect A all the way through to C? Think through the mechanism, not the vibe, before you look at the next slide.

questions.prompt: A subnet's route table contains only the automatic local route to the VPC's own address range. An engineer assigns a public IP address to an instance inside it. Is that instance now reachable from the internet?
options: Yes — a public IP address is always reachable regardless of routing.
No — with no route to an Internet Gateway, nothing in the path can deliver internet traffic to it.
Only if a NAT gateway also exists somewhere in the VPC.
Only if the subnet's name doesn't contain the word "private."

questions.prompt: VPC A peers with VPC B, and VPC B separately peers with VPC C. A resource in A needs to reach a resource in C. Will adding the right route table entries in B make that work?
options: Yes, once B's route tables point traffic correctly toward both A and C.
No — peering is non-transitive; A needs a direct connection to C, or all three need a Transit Gateway.
Yes, but only if all three VPCs are in the same AWS Region.
No, because peering connections expire automatically after 90 days.

scenes.narration: Here's why both of those go the way they do. The first one has no partial-credit answer: a public I P address with no matching route table entry changes nothing, because the routing decision happens independently of the address itself. The second is the non-transitivity trap in its purest form — peering connects exactly two VPCs, full stop, and no amount of clever routing in the middle VPC creates a path that doesn't exist. Once you need three or more VPCs reaching each other, that's a Transit Gateway's job, not peering's.

answers.prompt: Public IP address assigned, but no route to an Internet Gateway.
answers.correct: No — reachability is a route-table fact, not an IP-address fact.
answers.rationale: With only the local route present, nothing in the network path knows how to deliver traffic to or from the internet for that address. The public IP exists, but it's functionally inert until the route table itself sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway.

answers.prompt: A peers with B, B peers with C — does that connect A to C?
answers.correct: No — VPC peering is explicitly non-transitive.
answers.rationale: No route table configuration in B can make A↔C work, because peering only ever connects the two VPCs named in that specific connection. The real fixes are a direct A↔C peering connection, or replacing the mesh entirely with a Transit Gateway once more than a couple of VPCs need to reach each other.

scenes.narration: Five things to carry forward. Public and private are decided entirely by the route table, never by a flag or a public I P address. A NAT gateway only ever lets traffic out, never in. Security groups and network ACLs are deliberate opposites, and the exam tests them together far more than either alone. V P C peering never chains, no matter how the middle VPC's routes are configured. And V P C endpoints let you skip the NAT gateway entirely once the real destination is an AWS service instead of the open internet. Next chapter moves from where things sit on the network to what actually runs inside those subnets — EC2 instance families, purchasing options, and the real decision framework across EC2, Lambda, Fargate, and Batch.

props.heading: What to remember from this chapter
takeaways: Public vs. private is a route-table fact — a route to an Internet Gateway, never a subnet flag or a public IP address.
A NAT gateway is strictly one-directional: outbound-initiated traffic only, never an inbound door.
Security groups are stateful, instance-level, allow-only; NACLs are stateless, subnet-level, allow-and-deny — the exam tests them as a pair.
VPC peering never chains — A↔B and B↔C give you nothing between A and C without a direct link or a Transit Gateway.
VPC endpoints skip the NAT gateway entirely when the real destination is an AWS service, not the general internet.

scenes.narration: Before you move on, work this through yourself. A scenario says instances in a subnet must never accept an inbound connection from the internet, but must still be able to pull software patches whenever needed. Using exactly the mechanism from this chapter — what does that subnet's route table need to contain, and what must it never contain? There's one clearly correct route to add, and one route that, if you find it there, tells you the design already failed.

props.hint: Two specific things: one route it needs, one route it must never have.
